review:
Soaltee Crown in Kathmandu is beautifully and expansively located covering a huge area with good restaurants, a casino, and lush green gardens with a picturesque view of mountains in the background.  The hotel itself is beautifully decorated with traditional woodwork.  Its a pity that the combination of such a beautiful location and so much land under a prestigious hotel brand does not make up for some of the downsides of the hotel, which with a little more attention can be completely overhauled.  First of all, the rooms in some wings are damp and dark which gives them a certain shabby feel.  I stayed in June and since it was raining it was making it feel even more damp and gloomy.  The room amenities such as toilets and showers needed a retouch and fixing and these were not looked into till I started staying in the room.  The carpetings and upholstery didn't help the feel if not worsened.  I felt that for the price I was paying I wasn't getting as comfortable an accomodation.  I also felt that the hotel didn't utilize the acres of green it had under its wing properly as during my two weeks stay I didn't see much use of the outdoors other than to lounge around.  The hotel can do so much better by organizing outdoor bar-b-q's, open air entertainments etc.  This is especially needed for a hotel like Soaltee since it is a bit of a ride from the more happening areas of the city such as Thamel. 
The plus sides of the hotel are its friendly staff who demonstrated a nack for personal attention and the wonderful restaurants, specially the Chinese restaurant it has under its roof.  The other restaurants had great food too and so did room service.

THIS place is a peaceful oasis from the noisy bustle and crazy traffic which is Kathmandu.
The gardens are well laid out with several water features, colourful planting, graceful trees and a chance to relax in a little cafe area.
All that said, I still felt I was being discretely drained of as much money as the site could get out of me.
Entry cost R400 or about £2.40. This is not a lot of money but it is still a great deal by local standards for what might politely be called a "compact" garden.
The cafe then adds to the cost. Yes, you can ignore it, but a cool drink on a hot day is difficult to resist and that was another R170 or just over £1.
I didn't begrudge the money but I'm bound to say others sat round me grumbled at the cost which was a pity as I had spent a pleasant half hour walking round the gardens and enjoying a break from the busy merry-go-round of sightseeing in Kathmandu.
Overall I would say that a visit to the Garden of Dreams is worthwhile without being outstanding.

The first time I visited Devi's falls it was right at the height of monsoon (indeed it was raining when we went) and I was amazed!  This MASSIVE flow of water rushing straight at us, and then... POOF!  it disappeared down a big hole.  my friends and I spent some time wandering around for different view points to see where the water went.

The second time I had talked it up so much to some friends they were all buzzed, and then quite disappointed.  We came in May, at the end of the long dry season, and there was barely a trickle of water coming down the canyon (although now I could see the canyon itself, which was also interesting, geologically) and then going down a big black hole.  Interesting, but hardly mind-blowing.  the lack of water also revealed a lot of trash hung up on the rocks and plants surrounding the cave, which definitely took away from the mystique.  For a dry-season cave experience I recommend the Bat cave as my favorite natural attraction near Pokhara (some of the caves are closed during monsoon because of the water levels).

I give Devi's Falls 3 stars as an average for the two visits (excellent in monsoon, average in the dry season).  Bottom line, if you happen to be in Pokhara during Monsoon (June - September) it is worth a visit.

While it is a given that a 5 star hotel in Nepal will not possibly match up to what constitutes a 5 star in developed countries, this hotel sure does charge like one. And when you have paid more than what you would pay for a real 5 star even in India, of course you dont want to put up with what can at best be described as a 3 star. 
We had booked a club room (most expensive apparently) and the size of the room was smaller than even rooms in 2 star hotels and the bathroom absolutely tiny. My husband (at 6 feet) had trouble even moving around the bathroom properly to shave or shower.
Then comes the topic of the view from the room. We had to change rooms THRICE (for a 2 day stay). The first 2 times they gave us rooms facing the back of the hotel with the grand view being the hotel generators the sound of which was astounding. We insisted for a change and the room assigned yet again did not have a working AC!!!!!!
Absolutely fed up we asked to another change after waiting hours for a AC repairman and then were given a satisfactory room.
All rooms featured a CEMENT SLAB for a bed and it really was the worst bed I have slept in a hotel anywhere with any star. I had a fully body ache when I woke up both nights and it is strange why the hotel does not realize this!!
Another major problem with the hotel is its offbeat location, far away (7km to Thamel) so if you dont have a dedicated 24hr car its a hassle.
The much hailed breakfast buffet wouldnt even be called 'adequate' by international standards and the coffee served was absolutely below standard. The very expensive Italian restuarant (Al Fresco) can be described 'passable' at best. The swimming pool (scenic enough) was quite small.
The lobby washrooms were stinking and not even clean thus any claims to this hotel being a '5 star' could not be further from the truth.
The only pro to this hotel were the staff- always smiling and patient and ready to accomodate. Not a least irritated coping with a almost full hotel. They were the only pleasant part to the otherwise major disappointment the stay here was.

On 31 July 1961, a Swiss couple Davi went swimming but the woman drowned in a pit because of the overflow. Her body was recovered 3 days later in river Phusre with great effort. Her father wished to name it "Davi's falls" after her.

Its entrance fee is Rs 30/person. The fall is surrounded by metal fences for safety purposes. The fall is small with heavy flow of water. Hotel Shanker is located in an old colonial building about 10-15 minutes walk from Thamel. While situated nicely - away from the noise of Thamel, it is let down by the service.

- The Hotel in a guarded and gated compound so safety is pretty good. However, when walking back from Thamel at night, you will need to stay alert as you need to cross two busy roads.

- Service was a let down at the hotel. Check in staff were unhelpful and unfriendly.

- The rooms were large and clean but nothing exceptional. USB ports and universal power sockets were available which was a plus. Otherwise, the furniture and decor were functional but tired looking. 

- Wifi was available in the room. Speed was slow during peak times - breakfast and night.

- Breakfast was available each morning in a large dining hall. An egg station was available but was not particularly interesting. The highlight however were the different curries served each morning. 

- An outdoor pool is available - but unheated. Though perfectly fine after a day of walking the streets and temples.

- Typically, I don't go to the hotel restaurant for dinner. However, rather than crossing the busy roads at night, we stayed for dinner for one night. Food was good, though it was more Indian than Nepalese. The room service menu was different and significantly cheaper than the restaurant. If the weather is good, recommend having the room service meal delivered to you by the poolside.

Overall, the hotel is basic (by Western standards) and provides some sanctuary after a day of walking around the city. If the service improved, it would be even better.

review:
Devi's Fall is well known amongst the locals and tourists. Costs NPR 30 (20 for Nepalese citizens) to enter the site that has been poorly maintained (plastic bottles and rubbish every where). Does it worth NPR 30? I let you be the judge. It is not a huge fall: if you were expecting a Fall like Niagara, you'd definitely be disappointed. Go without any expectations.

Regardless, it is one of the point-of-interest in Pokhara. Your Pokhara visit cant be complete without visiting Devi's Fall.

It is said that Devi fell in the gorge and so it was called Devi's Fall.

If you prefer, follow these:

1. Take a short stroll along the lake side road (towards Basundhara Park) and go to Dam Side Park (ask locals how you can walk there) (15-20 mins walk). Cost: a coffee or cigarette for yourself.

2. Once you're done at the Dam Side Park, get out of the park, cross the road and wave at the next bus. Ask if the bus goes to Devi's Fall (some people also call it David Fall)

3. Get in the bus and ask the bus conductor to stop you near Devi's Fall. (Cost: NPR 30).

4. Once off the bus, look for the "Welcome to Devi's Fall" sign across the road. Go through little alley (entry cost: NPR 20 for Nepalese citizens, NPR 30 for all others).

5. Once you exit Devi's Fall and you're back on the road, cross the road and go to your right (say around 100yards/meters) and you will see the entrance to Mahendra Cave and Guptshwar Mahadev. Follow the signs: they are in English too (entry cost: NPR 10 for Nepalese citizens, NPR 30 for all others. If you see Kamadhenu cow as well, it is optional, it will cost additional NPR 10)

6. Once you're out on the road, go towards your left for about 250yards/meters where you can catch buses to the World Peace Pagoda (costs up to NPR 100). Ask the locals if you can't find the bus stand (there are no signs). No, don't walk to the Stupa unless you're in a big group. Walk is scenic but QUIET (less travelled) and steep. You never know what kind of people you may encounter on the way. Be safe than sorry!

7. Once out of the Stupa, catch a cab (costs NPR 800; 1000 max) to Lake side!

Voila!

First, the hotel web site was the very thing that convinced me to book at the Shanker. Also, my travel agent in KTM agreed that it's a fine place. Second, I would not stay in the Shanker again.

After a 6-day trek I wished for my son (age16) and I to stay in a nice place out of the center of the noise and chaos. Well, the Shanker delivered on the 2nd wish only. 

The hotel is a rip off - not worth the price you pay and not worth the nickels and dimes they charge for Wi-Fi and Internet in the grimy business center.

They charged us full rate for 2 nights even though we arrived 7pm Friday and checked out 10pm Saturday - no rated discount.

The small room itself had very hard beds (not a surprise) the bathroom had plenty of hot water but the grime and dirt everywhere was a real turn off. I did not see other rooms but may be, just may be they gave us a crappy room because we went through a local agent. 

The hallway carpets, furniture, doors, mirrors and walls were filthy. The lobby bathrooms are a disgrace. 

The restaurants are all in the "basement" of the hotel so they're dark and cavernous. 

The food was ok, they messed my steak order 2 times until I finally gave in a just ate it. The buffet breakfast is fine. A decent assortment of foods and the coffee was drinkable. 

The staff are moderately helpful - not terse - not unfriendly...just ok.

In my opinion the entire hotel needs to be gutted, scrubbed, re-furbished and re-fitted, then the image they promote will actually match the hotel value. 

And put a cafe or something in the gardens - why they're in the "basement" is beyond me. I asked about that and the concierge said that they're not in the basement they're on the ground floor. Well, technically that may be true but architecturally, they're in the basement.

It is well located - 15 minutes to the Int'l airport and a 20-minute walk to Thamel - if that is your scene.

The Shanker likely saw better days 50 years ago when it was first converted from a 19th Century Maharajah Palace but it seems that nothing has been done to it since that time.

Be careful if you are considering the Shanker. If that style is your thing, look elsewhere or try the new KTM Radisson down the road.

review:
We arrived around midday and were happy to be given a room a little early - however as we had just a basic room I wasn’t hugely impressed – it was rather small (by European standards) and looked onto concrete – perhaps because we’d paid a low internet rate but just beware they aren’t much like the pictures – so no duplex rooms on our floor. We didn’t try to change the room so perhaps others were better though the fire plan suggested our floor (2nd) were all the same. The bathroom was particularly small (think toilet between the bath and wall with no space at all between the two), however the water was hot. Internet was provided and free.

Breakfast was tasty enough, including an egg chef – in a large hall with light, however the evening before we tried to eat in the hotel’s restaurant which was a terrible idea; the food wasn’t great quality, was reasonably expensive and for some reason used a different room which was more like a bunker (no natural light). In addition there were only large tables there (for 6-20 people) and just as we, a couple, were finishing a (slightly) romantic meal they placed two other people right next to us… very surprising especially when we saw how much space they have elsewhere if they weren't just trying to crowd us in. There was a buffet option offered and though pricey for local standards it did appeal to the tour groups staying there.

So overall not a great experience but the building itself was rather lovely and we also had a welcome basket of fruit which was nice. Strangely I might consider returning as the hotel was a bit of an oasis in Kathmandu and a good location for our exploring (and looking to be outside Thamel), but would be a lot more careful of the room being chosen and would not eat there.
